qs.q: H2 receptor antagonists like ranitidine reduce gastric acid secretion by
o: Increasing prostaglandin synthesis in gastric mucosa
Blocking histamine stimulation of parietal cell H2 receptors
qs.e: H2 blockers competitively antagonize histamine at H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, preventing the histamine-mediated activation of adenylyl cyclase and subsequent stimulation of the proton pump. They do not directly block the pump itself (that's the mechanism of PPIs like omeprazole).

qs.q: Which of the following inhibits gastric acid secretion?
qs.e: Somatostatin is the 'universal inhibitor' in the GIT and directly inhibits parietal cell acid secretion.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: GIT Physiology Exam - April 21, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Potentiation in gastric acid secretion refers to:
o: The inhibition of Gastrin by Secretin
The synergistic effect of Acetylcholine, Gastrin, and Histamine
The role of the liver in neutralizing acid
The conversion of pepsinogen to pepsin
qs.e: Potentiation occurs when the combined effect of multiple stimuli (ACh, Gastrin, Histamine) is greater than the sum of their individual effects.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: GIT Physiology Exam - April 10, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which of the following hormones *inhibits* gastric acid secretion?
qs.e: Somatostatin, released by D cells in the stomach and duodenum, acts locally to inhibit gastrin release and directly inhibits parietal cell acid secretion, thereby decreasing gastric acid output.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: GIT Physiology Exam - March 27, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Regarding the regulation of gastric acid secretion, which statement is TRUE?
o: Antral distension primarily inhibits gastric acid secretion.
Histamine, released from ECL cells, is a potent stimulator of parietal cells.
Acetylcholine directly inhibits parietal cell function.
qs.e: Histamine, released from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in response to gastrin and acetylcholine, acts on H2 receptors on parietal cells, strongly stimulating HCl secretion.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: GIT Physiology Exam - March 27, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: The presence of fatty acids in the duodenum stimulates the release of which hormone that also inhibits gastric acid secretion?
qs.e: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released in response to fats and amino acids in the duodenum. Besides stimulating gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion, CCK also acts to inhibit gastric acid secretion and gastric emptying.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: GIT Physiology Exam - March 27, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which hormone has a primary role in decreasing gastric acid secretion when chyme enters the duodenum?
qs.e: When acidic chyme enters the duodenum, D cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum are stimulated to release somatostatin. Somatostatin acts to inhibit gastrin release from G cells, histamine release from ECL cells, and directly inhibits parietal cells, thereby decreasing gastric acid secretion as part of the negative feedback mechanism for the intestinal phase.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: GIT Physiology Exam - March 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Regarding the regulation of HCl secretion by parietal cells, which factor directly binds to its receptor on the parietal cell to stimulate acid secretion?
qs.e: Parietal cells have receptors for three main stimulators of acid secretion: acetylcholine (from vagal nerves), gastrin (from G cells), and histamine (from ECL cells). Somatostatin and prostaglandins inhibit acid secretion. So, acetylcholine is a direct stimulator binding to its M3 receptor on parietal cells.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Gastric acid is produced by parietal cells via the H+/K+ ATPase pump. Clinicians must understand the stimuli, regulation, and consequences of excess or deficient acid to diagnose and treat ulcer disease, dyspepsia, and related disorders.

sections.p: Acid secretion occurs in the stomach fundus and body, where parietal cells release HCl into the lumen. The acid creates a low pH that kills microbes, activates pepsinogen, and aids digestion.
b: Parietal cells use the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) as the final step.
Acid secretion is divided into basal, stimulated, and maximal phases.

sections.p: When stimulated, parietal cells exchange intracellular H+ for extracellular K+ using the proton pump, while Cl‑ follows passively, forming HCl.
b: Carbonic anhydrase generates H+ and HCO3‑ inside the cell.
HCO3‑ is exchanged for Cl‑ at the basolateral membrane (alkaline tide).

sections.p: Three main pathways drive secretion: neural (vagus → ACh), hormonal (gastrin), and paracrine (histamine). They converge on the proton pump.
b: ACh binds M3 receptors → PKC activation.
Gastrin binds CCK‑B receptors → Ca2+ rise.

t.b: Is hypergastrinemia present? High gastrin suggests gastrinoma or PPI overuse.
Is acid output excessive? pH <2 indicates hypersecretion; pH >4 suggests hyposecretion.

sections.p: Disorders arise from over‑ or under‑production of acid, each with distinct clinical patterns.
b: Peptic ulcer disease – excess acid erodes mucosa.
Zollinger‑Ellison syndrome – gastrin‑producing tumor → massive acid.

t.b: Distinguishes gastrinoma (very high) from PPI effect (moderately high).
Detects ulcer bleeding; positive result warrants urgent endoscopy.

sections.p: Understanding acid dynamics guides therapy for ulcer disease, GERD, and rare hypersecretory states, and informs safe use of acid‑suppressing drugs.
b: PPIs irreversibly block the H+/K+ ATPase – mainstay for ulcer healing.
H2 antagonists reduce basal and stimulated acid – useful when PPIs unavailable.
Sucralfate coats ulcers without altering pH – safe in pregnancy.

sections.p: Key points often tested: the three stimulatory pathways, the mechanism of PPIs, and diagnostic steps for Zollinger‑Ellison syndrome.
b: Identify which drug class targets the final step of acid secretion.
Know the diagnostic criteria for gastrinoma (fasting gastrin >1000 pg/mL, positive secretin test).
Recall complications of chronic hypochlorhydria (malabsorption, bacterial overgrowth).

whenToSeekHelp: Severe upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) – risk of shock.
Perforated ulcer with acute abdomen – surgical emergency.
Refractory ulcer pain despite PPI therapy – consider gastrinoma.

faq.q: Why do PPIs cause rebound acid hypersecretion after stopping?
faq.a: Chronic suppression leads to gastrin rise, stimulating parietal cells; when the drug is withdrawn, excess gastrin drives higher acid output.

faq.q: Can low‑resource settings diagnose Zollinger‑Ellison syndrome?
faq.a: Yes, by measuring fasting gastrin after stopping PPIs and performing a secretin stimulation test if available; otherwise, clinical suspicion guides referral.
It impairs protein digestion, reduces vitamin B12 absorption, and predisposes to bacterial overgrowth and infections.
